ITM820 · Academic project

Network Security Labs and the Complete Group Linux Service Project

Adnan Khan

I completed practical network-security labs and contributed to our Group 22 Linux project. This walkthrough covers packet analysis, file-integrity checks and the full group service workflow, from the Fedora VM and user accounts to web/database services, FTP, time synchronization, mail-client setup, PGP and SELinux.

Tools and environment

Wireshark; Windows command-line hash/checksum tools; PuTTY; TCP, HTTP, Telnet, SSH and TLS; VMware Workstation; Fedora; Apache, MariaDB, PHP, phpMyAdmin, Pure-FTPd, NTP, Evolution, Seahorse/GPG and SELinux.

Individual Assignments 1-4: Adnan Khan. Group 22: Abinayan Kokilan, Prathamdeep Multani, Adnan Khan and Tazwaar Alam. The group source does not allocate individual tasks. January-April 2026.

Follow a TCP upload from connection to data transfer

I identified client and server endpoints, followed SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK, and inspected the HTTP POST, acknowledgments and receive windows. An empty retransmission-filter view records no matches in that view. The assignment reported about 48 ms RTT and used 152,321 bytes over 0.236 seconds for its throughput calculation.

  • The reported throughput inputs give approximately 645,428 bytes/s, or 5.16 Mbit/s. They are coursework measurements, not a new replay of the capture.

Compare file integrity and HTTP authentication

I created ip.txt, calculated SHA-1/SHA-256 digests and a CRC checksum, changed the file and compared the values again. I also followed an HTTP 401 challenge and a later successful response. The exercise separates a content-change check from an authentication exchange.

  • SHA-256 output changes when the file changes. CRC is an error-detection comparison; neither an untrusted hash nor reversible Base64 encoding establishes authenticity or confidentiality.

Compare cleartext and encrypted sessions

I compared Telnet and HTTP observations with SSH and TLS traffic. Cleartext protocol fields can expose content; encrypted packet views still reveal useful connection metadata. The selected SSH evidence identifies encrypted packets without presenting captured credentials.

Build the group Linux environment and check networking

Our team documented VMware Workstation Pro 17 and a Fedora guest configured with 2 GB RAM, a 20 GB disk and NAT networking. We practised shell navigation, manual pages, hidden-file listings, interface inspection and DNS queries. Different later captures represent the coursework sequence rather than a verified single OS image.

Create users, groups and inspect access

Our group created local accounts, used a project group and inspected membership and file ownership. A regular-user attempt to enter /root returned Permission denied, providing a direct access-boundary observation. The account and group work established the identity context for subsequent service exercises.

Build the Apache, MariaDB and PHP stack

Our team installed the web and database components, completed MariaDB initialization steps and installed PHP. The PHP information page records the PHP component responding through the web stack. Each component has its own setup evidence; a browser response is stronger than a package command alone.

Add database administration and a protected web page

We installed phpMyAdmin and reached its login interface. The Apache exercise added directory authentication and an htpasswd account, restarted the service and tested the protected page. I distinguish the database login screen from the separate web-authentication exercise.

Publish and inspect FTP test content

Our team installed and started Pure-FTPd, prepared content and browsed the local FTP directory. The exercise used anonymous access in the lab. The directory and file views are evidence of the coursework test, not a secure production file-transfer design.

Configure time synchronization

We installed NTP, configured Fedora pool entries with iburst, started and enabled ntpd, and queried its peers. The peer output gives a recorded service check after configuration. Time-service setup belongs alongside the other operational dependencies of the lab.

Prepare the mail client and PGP identities

Our group checked the mail-related service, installed Evolution and configured account settings using POP on port 995 and SMTP on port 465. We also used Seahorse for PGP identities, key lists and keyserver lookup. These are configuration and key-management exercises; the source does not establish successful message delivery.

Inspect SELinux policy and login mappings

We installed policy tools, inspected sestatus and mapped the lab login to user_u with semanage. The resulting table records range s0. I describe the visible configuration as a targeted-policy/login-mapping exercise rather than an MLS enforcement result.

Bring the security and service checks together

The individual labs examine traffic and integrity. The team project adds accounts and services around those concepts. I used the evidence to distinguish setup, a reachable interface and a verified operation, rather than treating all three as the same result.

  • Troubleshooting: a denied /root operation required checking the current identity.
  • Packet analysis: connection flags, HTTP status and encrypted payloads answer different questions.
  • Service validation: mail delivery, decryption round trips and policy-enforcement tests would require additional evidence.

What I learned

  • Follow the evidence from transport setup to the application response.
  • Check identity, ownership and service state together when investigating access.
  • A service installation and a successful end-to-end transaction are different milestones.

Source: the full ITM820 portfolio supplied for this project. Evidence is from the original coursework; this edition adds no new lab test results. Repeated captures and earlier drafts are consolidated. Revised design summaries are labelled, and sensitive identifiers are masked.
